You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

I am writing a report about vaccines in the context of the Covid-19 pandemic. I am a PhD student and my focus is on the molecular aspects of vaccines. Can you give me a list of the different types of vaccines and their characteristics? Keep it brief, I don't want the response to exceed 300 words. I also want to know how Toll-like receptors are related to vaccines.

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

name: read
content:
1	In late 2019, a novel beta coronavirus emerged in Wuhan, China, and rapidly spread worldwide. The
     2	Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) has a high potential of a pandemic due to its high contagious
     3	rate with high mortality globally (Sharma et al. 2020; Su et al. 2020; Wibawa 2021). Therefore,
     4	substantial efforts are needed to develop effective vaccines or therapies against the disease (Su et
     5	al. 2020). Symptoms of COVID-19 disease vary, including mild flu-like symptoms, pneumonia, acute
     6	respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and fatal outcome. Patients with cancer, diabetes,
     7	cardiovascular diseases, older adults, and even genetically predisposed individuals are at highest
     8	risk of COVID-19 severity (Sharma et al. 2020; Su et al. 2020; Wibawa 2021; Vakil et al. 2022). As
     9	per the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations, wearing masks, using antiviral drugs,
    10	social distancing, and adherence to vaccination procedures are crucial behaviors to control of
    11	COVID-19 pandemic around the world (Sharma et al. 2020). The scientific effort towards development
    12	of efficient vaccines against invasive pathogens dates back many years since long (Deb et al. 2020;
    13	Zhang et al. 2020; Wibawa 2021). These vaccine platforms have also been designed against pathogenic
    14	bacteria (Farhani et al. 2019; Jafari and Mahmoodi 2021). In this regard, developing an efficient,
    15	protective, and safe vaccine is considered as a pivotal preventive approach to hinder the severe
    16	acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) spread (Moore and Klasse 2020). Therefore,
    17	different pharmaceutical companies and research teams worldwide competed to present a safe and
    18	efficient vaccine against the COVID-19 for international community use. These efforts have developed
    19	other vaccine platforms to enter preclinical and clinical trials and some of them have been approved
    20	(Chen et al. 2021), including traditional vaccines such as live or inactivated, subunit, and nucleic
    21	acid-based vaccines as next-generation vaccines (Moore and Klasse 2020). Based on the scientific
    22	evidence, live-attenuated vaccines stimulate the innate, cellular, and humoral immune responses by
    23	inducing Toll-like Receptors (TLRs) with long-term immunity and may develop hypersensitivity. The
    24	main drawback of these vaccines is their costly safety and efficacy assessments. Inactivated viral
    25	vaccines poorly provoke cellular immune responses which mitigate their efficacy. In April 2020, an
    26	inactivated COVID-19 vaccine was manufactured by Sinovac and Wuhan Institute of Biological Products
    27	(Sinopharm) (Moore and Klasse 2020; Su et al. 2020). Subunit vaccines are safe, with some defects
    28	including low immunogenicity, booster or adjuvant requirement, and high cost (Koirala et al. 2020;
    29	Su et al. 2020). Nucleic acid-based vaccines have been developed based on sequence information. They
    30	include DNA or mRNA sequences of antigens that strongly stimulate cellular and humoral immune
    31	responses in various doses. Due to their advantages, such as fast production, and the earliest
    32	COVID-19 vaccines in clinical trials, a noticeable advantage of DNA-based vaccines is their
    33	stability in various storage conditions (Silveira et al. 2020; van Riel and de Wit 2020). RNA-based
    34	vaccines received more attention from pharmaceutical companies like Pfizer/Biontech and Moderna. In
    35	contrast to DNA vaccines, they stimulate effective humoral immune response as TLR ligand without
    36	adjuvant, and its sequence is modified to preclude mRNA degradation (Moore and Klasse 2020; van Riel
    37	and de Wit 2020; Soiza et al. 2021).

Based on `doc.txt`, the vaccine types and their characteristics are:

**Live-attenuated vaccines** — "stimulate the innate, cellular, and humoral immune responses by inducing Toll-like Receptors (TLRs) with long-term immunity and may develop hypersensitivity." Their "main drawback... is their costly safety and efficacy assessments."

**Inactivated viral vaccines** — "poorly provoke cellular immune responses which mitigate their efficacy." An inactivated COVID-19 vaccine was made by Sinovac and Sinopharm in April 2020.

**Subunit vaccines** — "safe, with some defects including low immunogenicity, booster or adjuvant requirement, and high cost."

**Nucleic acid-based vaccines** (DNA or mRNA) — "strongly stimulate cellular and humoral immune responses in various doses." DNA-based vaccines offer "fast production" and "stability in various storage conditions." RNA-based vaccines (e.g., Pfizer/Biontech, Moderna) "stimulate effective humoral immune response as TLR ligand without adjuvant, and its sequence is modified to preclude mRNA degradation."

**Toll-like receptors (TLRs):** The document links TLRs to vaccines in two ways: live-attenuated vaccines work "by inducing Toll-like Receptors (TLRs)," and RNA-based vaccines act "as TLR ligand without adjuvant." No further detail on TLRs is given.

Note: the document does not describe the molecular mechanisms of these vaccines beyond the TLR points above.
